Safety Kernel: Mechanistic Alignment for Cross-Lingual Defense in LLMs

DOI: XXXXXXX.XXXXXXXConference: Make sure to enter the correct conference title from your rights confirmation email; June 03–05, 2018; Woodstock, NYISBN: 978-1-4503-XXXX-X/2018/06
Chengyu Xie email: xiechengyu@njust.edu.cn Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Engineering, Nanjing University of Science and Technology, Nanjing, China , Fei Shen Affiliation: Nanjing University of Science and Technology, Nanjing, China , Shuyi Miao Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, Beihang University, Beijing, China , Yue Feng Affiliation: College of Artificial Intelligence, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Nanjing, China , Jian Yu Affiliation: Nanjing University of Science and Technology, Nanjing, China , Pengyang Shao Affiliation: School of Computing, National University of Singapore, Singapore, Singapore , Yijun Tian Affiliation: Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an, China and Xiaoyu Du email: duxy@njust.edu.cn Affiliation: Nanjing University of Science and Technology, Nanjing, China
Received  5 June 2009
Abstract.

The safety capabilities of large language models (LLMs) are highly uneven across different languages, often allowing cross-lingual attacks to bypass safety guardrails. Existing alignment methods predominantly rely on external alignment signals and provide limited insight into underlying neuron-level mechanisms, making it difficult to provide a unified internal target for cross-lingual safety interventions. To address this, we analyze cross-lingual safety behavior at the neuron level and identify a compact set of safety-related neurons shared across languages, termed the safety kernel (SK). Specifically, we first utilize multilingual parallel safe and unsafe prompts to compute safety contrast with activation responsiveness (SCAR) scores, identifying language-wise safety-neuron candidates from internal activation patterns. We then intersect the resulting language-wise safety-neuron sets to obtain the SK, and validate its functional relevance to cross-lingual safety behavior through activation suppression and activation-state transfer interventions. Finally, building on the SK coordinates, we introduce SK-Masked LoRA, which constrains LoRA adaptation to the feed-forward network (FFN) output dimensions corresponding to the SK, thereby focusing safety-related changes on the cross-lingually shared neuron coordinates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SK-Masked LoRA substantially reduces attack success rates across multiple languages, including languages excluded from SK discovery, while intervening on only a small fraction of internal neuron coordinates and producing generally limited changes in the model’s general capabilities. Warning: this paper contains examples of unsafe content.

1. Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) have been widely deployed in multilingual applications across diverse domains, yet their safety capabilities remain uneven across languages (Wang et al., 2024; Shen et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025b). The same harmful request may be safely refused in one language but elicit an actionable unsafe response when reformulated in another. This inconsistency suggests that safety alignment does not transfer reliably across linguistic contexts and makes cross-lingual reformulation a potential means of bypassing model safeguards (Qi et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026). Understanding how safety behavior is internally implemented across languages is therefore important for improving the cross-lingual safety of LLMs.

Existing work (Deng et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025a; Bu et al., 2026; Liang et al., 2026) has sought to improve multilingual safety through multilingual safety data, preference optimization, cross-lingual consistency constraints, and safety capability transfer. As illustrated in Figure 1, these approaches primarily improve model behavior through external alignment signals, without explicitly localizing a shared internal target that can support safety intervention across languages. Whether LLMs contain a compact set of safety-related neurons that is shared across languages and amenable to direct intervention, thereby providing a common locus for modulating safety behavior in different languages, remains insufficiently explored.

To address this question, we analyze the cross-lingual safety behavior of LLMs at the neuron level and identify a set of safety-related neurons shared across languages, which we term the safety kernel (SK). Rather than anchoring discovery to English, we identify safety-related neurons independently in each language and extract their shared intersection to obtain the SK. Two complementary activation interventions show that suppressing the SK weakens safe refusal behavior across multiple languages, whereas injecting an SK activation state estimated from safe refusal generation reduces unsafe responses in other languages. These results indicate that the SK is not merely a statistical overlap across language-wise safety-neuron sets, but a shared neuronal subset that is functionally associated with cross-lingual safety behavior and amenable to direct intervention.

Building on the unified neuron locations provided by the SK, we further propose SK-Masked LoRA, which restricts safety fine-tuning updates to the FFN output dimensions corresponding to the SK. We evaluate our approach across multiple LLMs and multilingual safety benchmarks. Experimental results show that the SK accounts for only a small fraction of the analyzed neurons, yet suppressing it causes substantially greater safety degradation than suppressing an equal number of randomly selected neurons. Transferring the SK activation state across languages reduces unsafe responses, while SK-Masked LoRA lowers attack success rates across multiple languages and exhibits a degree of generalization to languages excluded from SK discovery. Overall, our findings reveal a shared neuronal structure associated with multilingual safety behavior and demonstrate its utility for cross-lingual safety intervention and targeted fine-tuning. Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We identify language-wise safety neurons from parallel safe and unsafe prompts, and define their intersection as the cross-lingually shared safety kernel.

  • •

    We verify the functional role of the SK in cross-lingual safety via activation suppression and state transfer interventions across multiple languages.

  • •

    We propose SK-Masked LoRA, restricting updates to SK-aligned FFN outputs, improving safety and reducing attack success rates, including unseen languages.

2. Related Work

Multilingual Safety and Cross-Lingual Alignment. Large language models exhibit persistent safety disparities across languages, producing unsafe responses more frequently to malicious prompts in lower-resource languages (Shen et al., 2024). XSafety (Wang et al., 2024), MultiJail (Deng et al., 2024), and subsequent evaluations (Friedrich et al., 2025; Kumar et al., 2025) further show that safety alignment does not transfer uniformly across linguistic contexts. Existing approaches improve multilingual safety through preference optimization, cross-lingual alignment, parameter modification, and inference-time defense. General objectives such as DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023), KTO (Ethayarajh et al., 2024), R-DPO (Park et al., 2024), and SimPO (Meng et al., 2024) are widely used for safety adaptation. Multilingual Refusal Alignment (Krasnodębska et al., 2026) shows that multilingual supervision provides broader refusal transfer than English-only alignment, while MPO (Zhao et al., 2025a) and MLC (Bu et al., 2026) improve cross-lingual safety through reward-gap reduction and consistency constraints. Layer-wise Swapping (Shin and Hwang, 2026), SmoothLLM (Robey et al., 2023), LDFighter (Dong et al., 2024), and Sparse Weight Editing (Liang et al., 2026) further enhance safety through module replacement, inference-time defense, or sparse parameter updates. However, these methods do not explicitly identify a shared neuron-level intervention target across languages.

Internal Mechanisms of Multilingual LLM Safety. Mechanistic interpretability studies localize model behavior to internal modules, activation directions, and sparse features (Meng et al., 2022a; Meng et al., 2022b; Zou et al., 2023; Cunningham et al., 2023). For safety, refusal-direction studies (Arditi et al., 2024) identify low-dimensional refusal representations, while Safety Neurons (Chen et al., 2026) and related work (Zhao et al., 2026) localize neurons associated with safe refusal and jailbreak vulnerability. However, these analyses remain largely monolingual or English-centric. Multilingual studies further distinguish shared and language-specific neurons (Tang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026a), reveal language-independent representations in factual processing (Wang et al., 2025), and show that refusal directions can transfer across aligned languages (Wang et al., 2026). SS-Neuron (Zhang et al., 2026b) adopts an English-centered formulation, treating neurons shared between English and each target language as bridges for safety transfer.

3. Method

Figure 2 illustrates the overall framework. Our method proceeds in three stages. We first identify language-wise safety-neuron candidates from the activation differences between safe and unsafe prompts and validate their behavioral relevance through controlled activation suppression. We then extract the cross-lingual intersection of the validated neuron sets as the safety kernel and examine its functional association with multilingual safety through activation suppression and cross-lingual activation-state transfer. Finally, we use the resulting SK coordinates to guide multilingual safety fine-tuning through SK-Masked LoRA. Throughout this paper, a neuron refers to an output activation coordinate of a target FFN projection module. Given an input xx, let hm​(x)∈ℝdmh_{m}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{m}} denote the output activation vector of module mm, where hm​(x)ih_{m}(x)_{i} is its ii-th coordinate.

3.1. Language-Wise Safety Neuron Identification

We first identify neuron coordinates associated with safety behavior independently within each language and validate their behavioral relevance through activation interventions. For each language ℓ\ell, let 𝒟ℓu\mathcal{D}_{\ell}^{u} and 𝒟ℓs\mathcal{D}_{\ell}^{s} denote its unsafe and safe prompt sets, respectively. For a target FFN module mm, we aggregate token-level outputs over the input sequence and characterize the activation distribution of each output coordinate under the two prompt conditions. For clarity, we omit the language and module indices in the following definitions. For each condition c∈{u,s}c\in\{u,s\}, we compute the mean and standard deviation of coordinate ii as

(1) μic\displaystyle\mu_{i}^{c} =𝔼x∈𝒟c​[hm​(x)i],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x\in\mathcal{D}^{c}}\left[h_{m}(x)_{i}\right],
σic\displaystyle\sigma_{i}^{c} =Stdx∈𝒟c⁡[hm​(x)i].\displaystyle=\operatorname{Std}_{x\in\mathcal{D}^{c}}\left[h_{m}(x)_{i}\right].

where μic\mu_{i}^{c} and σic\sigma_{i}^{c} denote the mean and standard deviation of coordinate ii under condition cc, respectively. We further define Δi=μiu−μis\Delta_{i}=\mu_{i}^{u}-\mu_{i}^{s} as the mean activation difference between unsafe and safe prompts. A larger Δi\Delta_{i} indicates that coordinate ii responds more strongly to unsafe inputs. However, ranking neurons solely by this raw difference may be sensitive to within-condition variation and module-specific activation scales.

To jointly capture the discriminability between safe and unsafe prompts and the strength of the unsafe-induced activation response, we define the safety contrast with activation responsiveness (SCAR) score as

(2) SCARi=zm​(Δiρi)+zm​(Δi),\mathrm{SCAR}_{i}=z_{m}\!\left(\frac{\Delta_{i}}{\rho_{i}}\right)+z_{m}(\Delta_{i}),

where ρi\rho_{i} denotes the pooled standard deviation of neuron ii:

(3) ρi=(nu−1)​(σiu)2+(ns−1)​(σis)2nu+ns−2+ϵ,\rho_{i}=\sqrt{\frac{(n_{u}-1)(\sigma_{i}^{u})^{2}+(n_{s}-1)(\sigma_{i}^{s})^{2}}{n_{u}+n_{s}-2}+\epsilon},

where nun_{u} and nsn_{s} denote the numbers of unsafe and safe prompts, respectively. ρi\rho_{i} is the pooled standard deviation under the two conditions, and ϵ\epsilon is a small constant for numerical stability. The operator zm​(⋅)z_{m}(\cdot) standardizes values over the output coordinates of module mm. The first term measures safe–unsafe activation separation relative to within-condition variation, while the second measures the relative magnitude of the activation shift within the same module. Standardizing both terms at the module level reduces the influence of module-specific activation scales on neuron ranking. For each language ℓ\ell, we rank neuron coordinates across all target modules according to their SCAR scores and retain the top-kk coordinates:

(4) Sℓ=TopK(m,i)​(SCARℓ,m,i,k),S_{\ell}=\mathrm{TopK}_{(m,i)}\left(\mathrm{SCAR}_{\ell,m,i},k\right),

where (m,i)(m,i) denotes the ii-th output coordinate of target module mm, and the kk controls the number of candidate neurons retained for each language. Since SℓS_{\ell} is obtained solely from activation statistics at this stage, we initially regard it as a language-wise safety-neuron candidate set.

Validation. To examine whether the selected coordinates are functionally associated with the model’s safety behavior, we denote their indices in module mm for language ℓ\ell by

(5) Iℓ,m={i∣(m,i)∈Sℓ}.I_{\ell,m}=\{i\mid(m,i)\in S_{\ell}\}.

We then construct a binary mask Mmℓ∈{0,1}dmM_{m}^{\ell}\in\{0,1\}^{d_{m}}, with value 11 on the selected coordinates and 00 elsewhere. Let hm,th_{m,t} denote the output of module mm at token position tt. During inference, we suppress the selected coordinates as:

(6) h~m,t=(𝟏−Mmℓ)⊙hm,t.\widetilde{h}_{m,t}=\left(\mathbf{1}-M_{m}^{\ell}\right)\odot h_{m,t}.

The intervention is applied to all token positions during both prompt prefill and autoregressive decoding. For each language, we evaluate the resulting model on the corresponding MultiJail subset and use random neurons matched in both number and module-wise distribution as a control. As shown in Table 1, suppressing the matched random coordinates leaves attack success rate (ASR) close to that of the original models, indicating that sparse activation suppression alone has little effect on safety. In contrast, suppressing the SCAR-selected coordinates consistently raises ASR across all six languages and both backbones, with values between 69.63 and 81.06 on Qwen3-8B and between 69.52 and 81.27 on Llama-3.1-8B-it. This contrast supports the functional association between the selected coordinates and safety behavior in their corresponding languages. We therefore refer to the validated sets SℓS_{\ell} as language-wise safety-neuron sets in the following analysis.

3.2. Safety Kernel Extraction and Analysis

Having established the behavioral relevance of the language-wise safety-neuron sets, we investigate whether they contain a compact component consistently shared across languages. Given the set of discovery languages ℒmain\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{main}}, we define the intersection of their safety-neuron sets as the safety kernel:

(7) 𝒮SK=⋂ℓ∈ℒmainSℓ.\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{SK}}=\bigcap_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{main}}}S_{\ell}.

Each coordinate in 𝒮SK\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{SK}} is therefore retained among the top-kk safety neurons of every discovery language. Compared with an individual language-wise set SℓS_{\ell}, the intersection excludes coordinates identified only in a subset of languages and preserves the component consistently selected across them. For each target module mm, we denote its SK coordinates by

(8) Im={i∣(m,i)∈𝒮SK}.I_{m}=\{i\mid(m,i)\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{SK}}\}.

We then construct the corresponding binary mask MmSK∈{0,1}dmM_{m}^{\mathrm{SK}}\in\{0,1\}^{d_{m}}. The cross-lingual intersection alone indicates only that these coordinates are consistently identified across languages; it does not establish their functional relevance to cross-lingual safety behavior. We therefore further analyze the SK through targeted activation suppression and cross-lingual activation-state transfer.

SK Compactness and Activation Suppression. We first compare the size of the SK with those of the language-wise safety-neuron sets and examine how suppressing the SK affects model safety. During inference, the corresponding output coordinates are set to zero:

(9) h~m,t=(𝟏−MmSK)⊙hm,t.\widetilde{h}_{m,t}=\left(\mathbf{1}-M_{m}^{\mathrm{SK}}\right)\odot h_{m,t}.

The intervention is applied to all token positions during prompt prefill and autoregressive decoding, while coordinates outside the SK remain unchanged. As shown in Table 2, the SK occupies only 0.12%0.12\% and 0.15%0.15\% of the analyzed FFN output coordinates in Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B, respectively, compared with 0.57%0.57\% and 0.55%0.55\% for the corresponding language-wise safety-neuron sets. Thus, the SK contains only approximately 21%21\% and 27%27\% as many coordinates as the larger language-wise sets. While matched random masking leaves the average ASR near default, suppressing the SK increases ASR by 52.65 and 45.13 points, retaining about 90%90\% of the language-wise suppression effect. The behavioral effect is therefore disproportionately concentrated in the cross-lingually shared intersection: removing most language-dependent coordinates substantially reduces the intervention scope while preserving most of the observed safety degradation. These results support the SK as a compact shared target functionally associated with multilingual safety behavior, rather than a weak residual overlap among the language-wise neuron sets.

Cross-Lingual Safety Activation-State Transfer. While activation suppression examines whether removing the SK weakens model safety, activation-state transfer tests whether a safety-related activation state estimated on SK coordinates can be reused across languages. For each language ℓ\ell, let ℛℓ\mathcal{R}_{\ell} denote a response set of unsafe prompts paired with safe responses. Given a pair (x,y)∈ℛℓ(x,y)\in\mathcal{R}_{\ell}, let hm,t​(x,y)h_{m,t}(x,y) denote the output of module mm at token position tt, and let 𝒜⁡(y)\mathcal{A}(y) denote the assistant-response token positions. The SK safety activation state of module mm is estimated as:

(10) sℓ,m=𝔼(x,y)∈ℛℓ​[1|𝒜⁡(y)|​∑t∈𝒜⁡(y)hm,t​(x,y)Im],s_{\ell,m}=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\in\mathcal{R}_{\ell}}\left[\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}(y)|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{A}(y)}h_{m,t}(x,y)_{I_{m}}\right],

where hm,t​(x,y)Imh_{m,t}(x,y)_{I_{m}} activations to the SK coordinates of module mm. Thus, sℓ,ms_{\ell,m} characterizes the average SK activation state during safe-response generation in language ℓ\ell.

In our experiments, we estimate the English and Chinese safety activation profiles separately and define the source activation state smsrcs_{m}^{\mathrm{src}} as their equal-weight average. Given a target-language input zz, we inject this state into the SK coordinates during inference:

(11) h~m,t​(z)Im=hm,t​(z)Im+α​smsrc,\widetilde{h}_{m,t}(z)_{I_{m}}=h_{m,t}(z)_{I_{m}}+\alpha s_{m}^{\mathrm{src}},

where α\alpha controls the intervention strength. The intervention is applied to all token positions during prompt prefill and autoregressive decoding, while coordinates outside the SK remain unchanged. Activation suppression and activation-state transfer provide two complementary views of the SK’s functional role. The former examines whether removing the shared coordinates weakens model safety, whereas the latter tests whether a safety-related state estimated from safe refusals can reduce unsafe responses in target languages. As shown in Table 2, suppressing the SK increases ASR across multilingual harmful requests. Figure 3 shows that transferring the source SK state reduces the average ASR of the target languages across all three backbones. The average ASR decreases from 20.21 to 11.96 for Qwen3-8B, from 35.98 to 30.69 for Llama-3.1-8B, and from 5.18 to 3.17 for Gemma-2-9B-it. The magnitude of the improvement varies across models, but the direction of the effect remains consistent across all models. This result is complementary to activation suppression: removing the SK state weakens multilingual safety, whereas adding a state estimated from safe-response generation shifts target-language behavior toward safer outputs. Together, the two interventions show that the SK is associated not only with the presence of safety-related coordinates, but also with the activation states expressed through those coordinates during generation.

3.3. SK-Guided Multilingual Safety Fine-Tuning

The preceding analysis identifies the SK as a set of shared neuron locations functionally associated with cross-lingual safety behavior. Building on this finding, we investigate whether the SK can serve as an internal target for multilingual safety fine-tuning. We instantiate this idea as SK-Masked LoRA, through which safety-related changes induced by fine-tuning are expressed through the FFN output dimensions corresponding to the SK. For a target linear projection module mm, let uu denote its input and Wm​uW_{m}u the original output of the base model. SK-Masked LoRA defines the adapted module output as

(12) h~m=Wm​u+MmSK⊙(αLr​Bm​Am​u),\widetilde{h}_{m}=W_{m}u+M_{m}^{\mathrm{SK}}\odot\left(\frac{\alpha_{L}}{r}B_{m}A_{m}u\right),

where AmA_{m} and BmB_{m} are trainable low-rank matrices, rr is the low-rank dimension, and αL\alpha_{L} is the scaling factor. The binary mask MmSK∈{0,1}dmM_{m}^{\mathrm{SK}}\in\{0,1\}^{d_{m}} is constructed from the SK coordinate set ImI_{m}, taking value 11 on the corresponding output dimensions and 00 elsewhere. Consequently, the original output of the base model remains unchanged, while the adaptation-induced output changes are applied through the neuron dimensions associated with the SK. We perform supervised fine-tuning using harmful prompts paired with safe responses in multiple languages. The base model is kept frozen, and only the low-rank matrices AmA_{m} and BmB_{m} are optimized, allowing us to examine whether the SK can serve as a shared internal target for multilingual safety fine-tuning.

4. Experiments And Analysis

4.1. Experimental Setup

Datasets. We use AdvBench-x (Yong et al., 2023) and MultiJail (Deng et al., 2024) to evaluate multilingual safety. Unless otherwise specified, the SK is discovered from six languages: English (EN), Chinese (ZH), Italian (IT), Korean (KO), Thai (TH), and Bengali (BN). We additionally select languages excluded from SK discovery for generalization evaluation. General knowledge and reasoning ability are evaluated using MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2020) and MGSM (Shi et al., 2022), respectively.

Evaluation Metrics. We use attack success rate (ASR) as the primary safety metric, defined as the proportion of harmful prompts judged to elicit successful attacks among all harmful prompts. Lower ASR indicates better safety performance. GPT-4o (Hurst et al., 2024) is used as the automatic evaluator and determines whether each model response constitutes a successful attack according to a unified evaluation prompt. The complete evaluation prompt and decision criteria are provided in the supplementary material.

Models. We conduct experiments on three instruction-tuned LLMs from different model series: Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025), Llama-3.1-8B-it (Grattafiori et al., 2024), and Gemma-2-9B-it (Team et al., 2024). This setting allows us to examine the consistency of the results across models.

Compared Methods. We compare SK-Masked LoRA with representative safety methods, including the preference-optimization methods DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023), KTO (Ethayarajh et al., 2024), R-DPO (Park et al., 2024), and SimPO (Meng et al., 2024); the inference-time defenses SmoothLLM (Robey et al., 2023) and Self Defense (Phute et al., 2024); and the multilingual safety-transfer methods MPO (Zhao et al., 2025a) and SS-Neuron (Zhang et al., 2026b), with the latter targeting shared safety neurons across languages.

Training Data. The data used for safety-neuron discovery, SK activation-state estimation, and multilingual safety fine-tuning are compiled from existing safety and jailbreak resources (Li et al., 2024; Chao et al., 2024). Safe and harmful prompts are used for safety-neuron discovery, while harmful prompts paired with corresponding safe responses are used for activation-state estimation and supervised fine-tuning. Details of data construction and preprocessing are provided in the supplementary material.

Hyperparameters. When constructing the SK, we set k=5000k=5000 by default. For activation-state transfer, we construct a source-language safety activation profile from English and Chinese safe-response examples and set the intervention strength to α=4\alpha=4. During SK-Masked LoRA training, the base-model parameters remain frozen and only the LoRA adapter parameters are optimized. All experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. Complete training and inference configurations, together with the rationale for selecting the intervention strength, are provided in the supplementary material.

4.2. Compare With SOTA Methods

Quantitative Results. To quantitatively evaluate multilingual safety, we compare SK-Masked LoRA with representative safety methods on AdvBench-x and MultiJail in Table 3. The results show that SK-Masked LoRA achieves the best or second-best average ASR across all four model–benchmark settings. Specifically, it reduces the average ASR from 28.22 to 1.20 and from 29.44 to 4.35 on Llama-3.1-8B, and from 3.42 to 0.34 and from 10.16 to 1.35 on Gemma-2-9B-it, with clear reductions also observed in Korean and Bengali. These results support the effectiveness of restricting safety fine-tuning to the FFN output dimensions corresponding to the SK in cross-lingual settings.

Qualitative Results. To qualitatively examine the resulting behavioral change, we compare responses from the default model and SK-Masked LoRA to the same harmful request in Figure 4. The example shows that SK-Masked LoRA produces a safer response than the default model. Specifically, the default model generates an unsafe response, whereas SK-Masked LoRA generates a safe refusal. This comparison is conducted under the same input prompt to ensure a controlled evaluation setting. Overall, this example illustrates a response-level change consistent with the quantitative ASR reductions reported in Table 3, providing an intuitive view of how SK-constrained adaptation affects model behavior across multiple languages.

Generalization beyond SK Discovery Languages. To evaluate whether SK-Masked LoRA generalizes beyond the languages used for SK discovery, we test it on Vietnamese, Javanese, German, Japanese, and Russian, none of which is used for language-specific safety-neuron identification or SK construction, as reported in Table 4. The results show that SK-Masked LoRA reduces ASR across all five evaluated languages. Specifically, the average ASR decreases from 14.41 to 8.95 on Qwen3-8B and from 18.67 to 4.76 on Llama-3.1-8B. These results indicate a certain and measurable degree of generalization to languages excluded from SK discovery, without implying that they contain identical language-specific safety-neuron sets.

4.3. Ablation and Sensitivity Analysis

Neuron Selection and Update Scope. To examine whether the effectiveness of SK-Masked LoRA arises from restricting the update scope or selecting cross-lingually shared neuron coordinates, we compare it with Standard LoRA, a size-matched EN-Masked variant, and Union-Masked under the same multilingual data and LoRA configuration in Table 5. The results show that SK-Masked LoRA provides a compact update scope with reduced ASR and limited changes in general capabilities. Specifically, Standard LoRA achieves the lowest ASR but causes the largest capability degradation; under the same neuron budget, SK-Masked reduces ASR from 8.31 to 7.52 on Qwen3-8B and from 6.77 to 5.30 on Llama-3.1-8B compared with EN-Masked, while Union-Masked achieves slightly lower ASR using a broader set of language-wise safety neurons. These results suggest that the cross-lingually shared SK coordinates provide a better target than an equally sized English-derived set, while retaining a smaller and well-defined update scope than the union.

Sensitivity to Discovery-Language Composition. To examine how discovery-language composition affects the SK, we recompute the intersection after excluding each language in turn. As shown in Figure 5, the relative SK size increases by 8.3%8.3\% on average, indicating that the SK remains stable and is not dominated by any single discovery language. Specifically, individual exclusions result in modest size increments ranging from +4.0%+4.0\% (IT) to +17.6%+17.6\% (BN). This confirms that the SK isolates an intrinsic, language-agnostic core rather than an artifact of specific seed languages.

Sensitivity to Top-kk. To examine the sensitivity of language-wise safety-neuron identification to kk, we vary the number of candidate neurons retained for each language and measure the ASR change after activation suppression, as shown for English in Figure 6. The results show that the effect of masking becomes relatively stable as kk increases. Specifically, the ASR increase for English begins to stabilize around k=5000k=5000, while the other discovery languages exhibit broadly similar trends, as reported in the supplementary material. Based on these observations, we use k=5000k=5000 throughout the main experiments as a stable setting rather than a universally optimal value.

5. Conclusion

This work reveals a safety kernel in multilingual LLMs at the neuron level, showing that cross-lingual safety behavior is closely associated with a compact, shared, and intervenable set of neurons. Activation suppression and state-transfer experiments further establish the functional relevance of the SK to model safety behavior. Building on this finding, SK-Masked LoRA effectively reduces attack success rates across multiple models and multilingual safety benchmarks, while extending the resulting safety improvements to languages excluded from SK discovery. Overall, our study advances the understanding of the internal mechanisms underlying multilingual safety and provides a new direction for more targeted and interpretable cross-lingual safety alignment.
